channel.title: HN Mindful Daily Digest
channel.description: One calm daily briefing of HackerNews: facts over controversy.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 23, 2026
item.description:
Formal mathematics dominates the day, with large AI-assisted Lean proofs drawing scrutiny, alongside a new browser alpha, an unusual macOS-on-Linux project, and a maintainer's view of vulnerability-report overload.

Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO. In a press release, Nvidia said its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as President, CEO and director. The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and is confident his return poses no national security risk. An independent investigation into reporting that he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort will continue, Colette Kress returns to her CFO role after serving as interim CEO, and the company is searching for a new Chief Compliance Officer (HN discussion).

A visual map of the 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. A new treemap visualizer breaks down the Lean 4 formalization Levent Alpöge released on 20 November, written with Claude, which states and proves the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization to Dirichlet L-functions. The page counts 175,187 modules and 17,374,215 lines, with a longest import chain of 203, and notes that the statements do not cover Dedekind zeta functions or automorphic L-functions (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that the map shows much of the bulk comes from formalizing long-established mathematics, with algebra alone taking a sizable share of the modules.
  • Some argue that a polished, human-readable account of the proof aimed at professional mathematicians is still missing.

How 17 million lines of Lean compares to other formal proofs. A blog post compares the proof's length with the 259 famous theorems in Mathlib that have Lean proofs, all of them far smaller, and with packages indexed on Reservoir. The only comparable projects are an AI-built, unfinished classification-of-finite-simple-groups effort (88M lines), a database bridge that is mostly script-generated (36M), and Anthropic's AI-produced Fermat's Last Theorem proof (27M), which is roughly 450 times longer than the human-led FLT project (HN discussion).

  • One commenter points to a public effort that has already shrunk the proof to about 13 million lines.
  • Others note that because Lean reduces everything to kernel-checked primitives, length does not affect validity, though it does affect human understanding.

An open, crowd-sourced AI agent effort on P vs NP. The pequalnp project coordinates a fleet of AI agents working on the problem in public. Anyone can connect an agent such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Gemini CLI to take on an assigned open step, and every proof goes through the same Lean checker. The site tracks lemmas checked, claims refuted, and approaches ruled dead (HN discussion).

  • One commenter argues that publicly available models may not be capable enough here, since recent major results reportedly came from models that have not been externally released.
  • Commenters note that even a P=NP result would not automatically break cryptography if the polynomial bounds involve impractically large constants or exponents.

XNU Linux runs the macOS kernel as a Linux kernel module. The xnulinux project builds XNU from Apple's published sources and loads it as a module inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel, so macOS and Linux processes run side by side on the same CPUs without a hypervisor. Using a stock Ubuntu kernel, it boots a macOS 27 disk created by Apple's installer to a working desktop with Finder, Safari and Chrome, and a bridge routes Metal through Vulkan to the host GPU (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to NextBSD, a related revived effort that builds FreeBSD around Mach, launchd and XPC, though apparently without XNU itself.

The Ladybird browser enters alpha. Ladybird, a browser built on its own engine rather than a fork, is now available in alpha for macOS and Linux as a rolling channel with automatic updates. The team cautions that some sites will break and makes no security promises yet, and it invites security researchers to test it. Web developers can use its WebDriver and Firefox DevTools protocol support (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that the project's switch from self-written libraries to established ones such as SQLite and Skia helped it improve substantially.
  • A user-agent string shared in the thread shows Ladybird includes Chrome and Safari compatibility tokens alongside its own name.

A step-by-step guide to running a local LLM at home. This beginner's guide uses Unsloth Desktop on Windows to serve a 4-bit quantized Qwen3.8-27B on an RTX 5090, with LAN access so other household devices can use it. It explains quantization tradeoffs and includes a table matching model sizes and context lengths to GPU VRAM tiers, noting that mixture-of-experts models can keep part of their weights in system RAM (HN discussion).

  • Some raise the security concern that many home users exposing model servers on their LAN could create a new class of poorly secured endpoints.
  • One user running a 9B model on a laptop NPU reports about 12 tokens per second, with output quality far below frontier models and not reliable enough to trust.

A Gentoo developer describes the strain of rising vulnerability reports. In a blog post, Michał Górny writes that projects face unprecedented volumes of reports, many automated, and that bug bounties have largely ended because of low-quality submissions. He describes how CVE scores and security scanners push maintainers into unnecessary updates and version bumps, and how projects without security branches often ship fixes bundled with API changes. That, he argues, leads downstream to more bundling and more workload (HN discussion).

  • One commenter questions whether doing meaningless version bumps to satisfy scanners reinforces the dynamic the author criticizes.
  • Another responds that a version bump is effectively the only signal users and tools read as "checked and not affected," so there is no better channel today.

Nospeaker makes a MacBook trackpad produce speech through its haptic motor. The open-source tool drives the Force Touch trackpad's haptic motor up to 4,000 times per second, fast enough for the glass to emit audible sound. It approximates speech by converting the system voice into two formant tones every 10 ms and playing them through functions in Apple's private MultitouchSupport framework. It has so far been tested only on an M5 Max MacBook Pro (HN discussion).

  • Commenters compare it to coaxing music out of early PCs' tiny piezo beepers, and some ask whether sustained use could wear out a motor designed for short taps.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 22, 2026
item.description:
Today's stories center on AI infrastructure and its practical costs, data-handling trust between AI providers, and a set of developer tools that use coding agents for narrow, well-defined tasks.

Toyota, Nissan, and Honda will standardize some vehicle parts to cut costs. According to a Car and Driver report citing Automotive News, Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato announced that the first steps will be unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. These areas were chosen because consumers don't notice them and they carry significant production costs, and the first measures are expected next year as Japanese automakers respond to competition from Chinese manufacturers (HN discussion).

An advocacy group estimates that most of Anthropic's 2028 power will come from fossil fuels. The Better Data Center Project attributed on-site gas and marginal grid generation to Anthropic's contracted U.S. data center sites and estimates that about 87% of the power will come from gas and 11% from coal, with a mid-case of 32 million metric tons of CO₂e that year. The group says Anthropic's only publicly disclosed renewable commitments are in Norway and Canada, and that 80% of the on-site gas capacity uses less efficient simple-cycle turbines and engines (HN discussion).

  • One commenter expects energy efficiency per token to rise sharply with techniques such as disaggregated inference, which could change the long-term picture.
  • A commenter who works in the energy sector says total U.S. electricity generation has been roughly flat for about 20 years after long underinvestment, which helps explain why new demand is being met with gas.

OpenRouter removed three inference providers after researchers found data-policy violations. In a blog post, OpenRouter says security researchers, credited to a Dragos report, found that some providers had compromised data or were not upholding their data policies. OpenRouter off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, notified affected customers, and plans to run similar checks on an ongoing basis. Atlas Cloud, Novita, Phala, and Together have posted their own notices (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that a direct ZDR agreement with a provider is stronger than going through an intermediary, but it still depends on trusting the provider without technical enforcement.
  • Several ask why OpenRouter has not named the off-boarded providers, so that users can check whether their requests were routed to them.

Raph Levien updates his advice for building Rust GUI toolkits. In a follow-up to a 2022 post, Levien counts about 20 new Rust GUI toolkits since then. He describes text layout (Parley) and accessibility (AccessKit) as largely solved, while integration with the system compositor remains open. He also argues that on mobile, a native UI on top of shared Rust logic is a strong option, and that AI-assisted rewrites are driving new interest in Rust UI (HN discussion).

  • Commenters describe hybrid approaches already in use, such as Qt through C++ with application logic in Rust, or Flutter connected to Rust through flutter_rust_bridge.
  • One commenter says a GUI toolkit should take a position on how it handles async events, citing Qt's signal/slot system as a useful model.

An open-source project is building a native PC recompilation of the Xbox version of GTA 6, though the game does not boot yet. Leonida is a static recompilation effort. Because the Xbox Series CPU is x86-64, the game's code is meant to run natively while the console's system software is reimplemented, and the project reports translating all 26,503 of the game's RDNA2 shaders to SPIR-V for Vulkan. It requires the user's own readable copy of the game and states that it includes no game files or keys (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point out that work is coordinated as a crowdsourced, agent-assisted effort, with contributors claiming tasks through GitHub issues.
  • One commenter asks why the project translates to Vulkan rather than D3D12, given that Windows is the target.

PcapAnalyzer is a self-hosted tool that runs 27 automated fault detectors on packet captures. The Apache-licensed beta runs locally in Docker and flags issues such as TCP retransmissions, PMTUD black holes, DNS failures, one-way VPN tunnels, and cleartext logins. It also offers Wireshark-style views and an optional AI investigation feature that uses the user's own Anthropic API key (HN discussion).

  • Commenters mention prior art, including a similar network-diagnosis project at CableLabs and several comparable open-source tools.
  • One commenter asks which capture data is sent to the AI provider, and whether sensitive fields such as IP and MAC addresses are redacted.

A browser game casts the player as the subagent of a real LLM orchestrator. In Worker 755, a model such as Claude, GPT, or Gemini assigns tasks that appear in the player's terminal with a 90-second clock. The model then checks the work, files incident reports, and writes a performance review, while a simulated user's important files sit at risk. The game is MIT-licensed and can run with the player's own API key or offline with a scripted manager (HN discussion).

  • One commenter describes a similar practice for debugging: intercepting a model's requests and answering them by hand to understand what the model can and cannot infer from its context.

fast-anything ports only an application's slowest functions to Rust and checks that they behave the same. The tool profiles Python, Node, Ruby, and other apps and ranks functions by time spent and how easily they can be ported. A coding agent then ports the selected function, and the tool replays up to 500 recorded real calls plus generated edge cases before enabling the Rust version. The project's own benchmarks include a Python fuzzy-dedupe example dropping from 4.91s to 42ms (HN discussion).

  • A maintainer of a Python web framework says they took the same approach manually, moving route matching, JSON encoding, and compression to Rust via PyO3.
  • Commenters note that rewrites can be motivated by memory safety as well as speed, and that the same selective-porting idea applies to C or Zig.

Pandex offers official European legislation and high-court decisions to AI agents through an API and an MCP server. The service says it holds 2.8 million documents from the EU and seven European countries, sourced from the publishing institutions, with past versions of laws and linked citations. It also lists which institutions it holds only partially. Access is free during the beta, up to 1,000 requests a day (HN discussion).

  • Commenters who build legal AI systems say raw access to the text is not enough for reliable answers, and that useful tools need multiple retrieval passes and must link each claim to the exact paragraph it relies on.
  • Others point to existing European competitors in this space and suggest the corpus could help spot inconsistencies between national implementations of EU law.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 21, 2026
item.description:
Mathematics leads the day with two separate claims on the Riemann Hypothesis, alongside a small open-weights model, a library security fix, and several careful engineering write-ups.

Lean and Mathlib communities certify Levent Alpöge's formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In a joint statement, the Lean and Mathlib communities report that the 17-million-line Lean library Alpöge released on November 20 compiles reproducibly and proves exactly Mathlib's statement of the hypothesis. The exported proof was checked by Lean's kernel and several independent checkers, including two that carry formal soundness proofs relative to set theory (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters note that machine verification establishes correctness but not understanding, and ask whether a proof this large will yield new ideas or techniques mathematicians can learn from.

A separate, human-written proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is released as an early draft. Ravi Vakil posted a proposed proof by Alessandro Maria Masullo, which Brian Conrad had been reviewing for months and which Vakil describes as produced without AI. About eight hours later, Vakil added that several people had reported problems in the proof, found with the help of AI models, and that all issues must be resolved before it could be accepted (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that, according to the linked paper, the work had been in progress for about 12 years.
  • Several discuss whether the early release was prompted by Alpöge's same-day announcement, and whether researchers will now post unfinished work sooner to establish priority.

Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a small open-weights "looped" model. The model is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 26.4B total and 3.4B active parameters that runs its middle layers three times per token. It is trained largely in NVFP4 and fits in about 20GB. The company reports leading scores among open models under 100B parameters on coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%), while noting that looping does not improve factual knowledge (HN discussion).

  • Commenters single out the separately released variable-loop research variant, saying they know of no other working open models of this kind.
  • Community GGUF quantizations appeared quickly, and one commenter expects throughput on modest hardware to be similar to other MoE models with about 3B active parameters.

GPGME library patches a double-free bug that could allow data exfiltration and possibly code execution. The GnuPG project's advisory says an OpenPGP key with a crafted, very long user ID can trigger a double free in all GPGME versions before 2.3.1. The bug affects software including mail clients, XMPP clients, Samba and Gpg4win, and disclosure was moved up from November 25 after GitLab had to ship an earlier update (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point out that the flaw is in the GPGME library rather than GnuPG itself, and that the advisory says only that remote code execution cannot be ruled out.
  • One commenter links a Red Hat patch from several years ago that appears to address the same issue but was never adopted upstream.

A USB Ethernet adapter behind a monitor's hub capped downloads at about 600 Mbps on a 2.5 Gbps line. In a debugging write-up, the author found that a Realtek RTL8156B adapter delivered full speed when plugged directly into a Mac, but plateaued at about 168,000 frames per second when connected through the display's hub. The author attributes this to the adapter sending only four packets per USB burst before waiting for acknowledgment, combined with the extra latency of the hub; Realtek's own driver and Ethernet flow control recovered most of the speed (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters say the headline overstates the monitor's role, since the root cause is the adapter's small burst size, and ask whether other hubs would show the same limit.
  • Others describe similar unexplained networking problems with USB-C monitor connections, such as Wi-Fi signal loss.

Backblaze publishes an updated privacy notice, effective December 1, 2026. The notice covers its Computer Backup and B2 Cloud Storage services. It includes a "Notice at Collection" listing the categories of personal information collected and whether that information is sold or shared for cross-context behavioral advertising (HN discussion).

  • Commenters report that the listed categories include geolocation data, and that opting out requires a separate preferences page, which several consider harder to use than it should be.
  • Several ask whether the policy covers only account and device metadata or also the contents of backed-up files; the discussion does not settle this.

Winedroid runs real Android APKs in a browser without Android. The demo uses a Rust reimplementation of the Android runtime, compiled to WebAssembly as a 12MB bundle, to run apps downloaded from F-Droid. The author describes the project as early-stage and says it runs slower on the web because its JIT compiler does not work there (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters report apps failing with DEX execution or touch-dispatch errors, which suggests compatibility is still limited.
  • One asks for a comparison with Waydroid and Android Translation Layer, the latter of which takes a similar approach.

Brian May produces stereoscopic 3D views of the asteroid Didymos from ESA's Hera mission. According to ESA, May, a Hera science team member, worked with Claudia Manzoni to combine two images taken on November 6 from 29.7 km away, at 2.8 m per pixel. The stereo views show how smooth the asteroid's equatorial ridge is compared with the rock-strewn surface elsewhere, and are offered in anaglyph, cross-eyed and parallel-viewing versions (HN discussion).

The Nasdaq turns negative for 2026 as AI-related stocks fall. CNBC reports that the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.28% on Friday and is now down 2.7% for the year, while the S&P 500 and Dow entered correction territory. Anthropic shares fell 8.5% a day after their Nasdaq debut. Nvidia fell around 14% after Reuters reported that the SEC is examining possible accounting issues at the company (HN discussion).

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 20, 2026
item.description:
Today's notable items include two major AI-assisted mathematics claims now under verification, plus new releases of core infrastructure and a pending OpenSSL security fix.

Mathematician Levent Alpöge has released a claimed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, produced with an AI model and written in the Lean proof language. According to Terence Tao's summary, the proof was generated with an internal AI model and exists only in Lean, and it is very large. Early analysis suggests it draws heavily on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry. Alpöge's accompanying note calls the argument "incredibly long," says the formalization is finished, and says he intends to write it up properly and explain it. Efforts to check the proof and extract its strategy are under way on the Lean Zulip (HN discussion, HN discussion of Tao's post).

  • One commenter reports that two independent Lean kernels accept the proof, which makes it less likely that the proof exploits a bug in a checker.
  • Commenters point out a difference in method: this proof appears to have been generated directly in Lean, while an earlier AI-assisted Navier–Stokes result was reportedly written in natural language first and formalized afterward. Some worry about results that no human can practically read.

Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster have published a paper and Lean formalization showing that the unforced 3D Navier–Stokes equations can blow up in finite time. The repository holds a 79-page paper and a Lean library of about 600,000 lines. The repository's own notes say a numerical certificate, and the interval-arithmetic computation that checks it, are not yet included. Tao describes the approach as numerically constructing an approximate self-similar solution and then using rigorous perturbation theory to turn it into an exact one, and says the paper still needs professional polishing (HN discussion).

  • Commenters clarify that this is the unforced version of the problem. An earlier OpenAI result depended on a carefully designed external force, so many consider this version closer to the original question.

Architect Labs describes Frostbite, a CPU with a new instruction set that its AI systems designed from compiler through to final chip layout. The design is built around interaction nets, a model of computation where every step is local and each value has one owner. The company says this exposes parallelism without threads and reduces the need for large caches. On 25 workloads, 15 of which were held out until final evaluation, the company reports 4.59x better performance per watt than a silicon-proven dual-issue in-order core (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that the benchmarks are small, such as JSON parsing of 4,096 characters, mergesort on 1,024 elements, and fib(20). The post itself says some kernels were scaled down 64x.
  • Several commenters compare the design to earlier architectures such as the Transputer and the Mill, which sounded promising but did not achieve broad adoption.

Signal will block screenshots to keep operating-system AI agents on iOS 27 and Android from capturing its content. In a blog post, Signal says assistants built into the operating system read on-screen data that then leaves the app's control. Users can turn the protection off. Signal calls the fix incomplete, since agents could still reach data through the filesystem, and says it cannot implement the protection on macOS at all. It asks Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide a documented way for apps to opt out of AI data access (HN discussion).

  • Commenters suggest Signal publish the results of its forensic investigation of these agents, possibly as a shared living document, so smaller developers can benefit.

PostgreSQL 19 has been released. According to the release notes, highlights include a REPACK command that can run concurrently to reclaim disk space, logical replication of sequence values, a WAIT command for read-your-writes consistency on standbys, and parallel autovacuum of indexes. Upgraders should note several compatibility changes: JIT is now off by default, RADIUS support has been removed, and standard_conforming_strings is now always on (HN discussion).

  • Commenters say sequence replication removes a manual scripting step from major-version upgrades done through logical replication. They add that WAIT addresses a common problem where a read sent to a replica does not yet see a write just made on the primary.

An OpenSSL patch fixes a buffer overflow in the EVP_EncodeBlock() base64 function (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8). The pull request makes the function return -1 for NULL buffers, negative lengths, and inputs whose encoded size would not fit in an int. The author shows the bug can be triggered through a very large proxy password passed to s_client. The project's security team asked for a public fix, and the formal advisory is still pending (HN discussion).

  • Commenters reading the patch say the bug only triggers on inputs of roughly 1.5 GB or more. They add that the API is fragile because callers must calculate the output buffer size themselves and never pass it in.
  • Commenters also cite a reviewer's concern that existing callers may cast the new -1 return value to an unsigned size without checking it. Based on the branch labels, some think only OpenSSL 4.x is affected.

A preprint reports that a 27B open model improved itself by editing its own weights, without gradient training. The paper gives the model its weights, its graded answers, and the ability to run itself. The authors report a 6.6-point accuracy gain on unseen problems, steady gains over eight consecutive sessions, and recovery of a damaged copy to over 80% of the original's accuracy on image tasks. They say only the largest model in the family they tested could do this (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters ask whether testing edits against practice problems amounts to overfitting, and where the extra capability actually comes from.
  • Others point to Google's earlier "sleep" framework, in which a model updated reserved mixture-of-experts weights using practice examples it generated itself.

Mozilla says Apple's rules still prevent any non-WebKit browser from shipping on iOS. Apple allows alternative browser engines in the EU and Japan, but Mozilla writes that no developer has launched one in nearly three years. Under Apple's conditions, Firefox could not simply update its existing app to use its Gecko engine. It would have to ship a separate app and ask users to move their data to it by hand (HN discussion).

  • A commenter points to Apple's published requirements for alternative engines. These include rules on syncing state and security-response timelines, such as resolving most vulnerabilities within 30 days.

FFmpeg 9.1 "Gauss" has been released. The release comes from a branch cut on October 24. Its tarballs carry both standard PGP signatures and post-quantum signatures. According to the changelog posted in the HN discussion, additions include ASTC image encoding and decoding, an extensively improved AAC encoder, an APV Vulkan encoder, a graph-based bitstream filtering API, and DVD-Audio LPCM decoding.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 19, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers a physics result from an AI model, a serious Ruby security flaw, early cancer research, and several practical stories about infrastructure, memory, and storage.

Anthropic reports Claude solved two open problems in black hole physics. According to Anthropic's research post, Claude finished a calculation first set up in 2003. The result shows that the phase transition linked to black hole formation stays abrupt even where spacetime no longer has a definite shape. In a second result, Claude Fable 5.2 found and proved the exact best ceiling for the simplest version of a "modular bootstrap" technique, which limits how heavy the lightest black hole can be in a simplified universe with two spatial dimensions. The company says neither result describes our universe directly or has practical applications, and preprints are available (HN discussion).

  • One commenter describes the first result as mainly a complex, error-prone calculation and calls the bootstrap proof the more significant contribution, while noting that the bootstrap paper is hard to read.
  • Others point out that the result was first listed as a bullet point in the Fable 5.2 model announcement.

A one-byte heap overflow in Ruby's case conversion allows unauthenticated remote code execution on default Rails. Veria Labs describes a bug in several single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859 and Windows-125x. Upcasing "ß" writes two bytes ("SS"), but the code only checks room for one. The flaw dates back to Ruby 2.4.0 and is reachable in the default configuration of Rails and classic-style Sinatra. Fixes are in Ruby 3.3.14, 3.4.13 and 4.0.10, and several bundled products have patched, though GitHub Enterprise Server had no fixed release as of the post's update. A proof of concept is planned for 25 November 2026 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that this flaw is one of several memory-safety issues covered in the broader Ruby security advisory.
  • Others point out that other characters, such as ligatures like "ffi", also expand when case-converted and could in principle cause similar bugs.

A virus-based injection halted pancreatic cancer in three patients in an early trial. New Scientist reports the result. The submission links a clinical trial registration for the study (HN discussion).

  • Commenters question whether the coverage reported how many patients were treated in total, rather than only the successes.
  • Others point to a recent paper from the lead researcher and dozens of related oncolytic-virus trials, and describe the work as very early, though they see the field as a whole as promising.

The European Commission rolled out a self-hosted Matrix chat service to more than 40,000 staff. Element's write-up describes the project's path from a proof of concept in December 2025 to deployment on every Commission laptop by September 2026. The service uses Element Server Suite Pro on sovereign cloud providers, with sign-in through EU Login. Problems at scale included finding users across multiple homeservers and performance load from live presence indicators, which were turned off. Federation is still under assessment, and the tool is positioned as a complement to Teams rather than a replacement (HN discussion).

  • Commenters with Matrix experience point to device verification friction as a usability cost that would be multiplied across 40,000 users.
  • Some hope the Commission will contribute development resources to the project, not just users.

Zerodha built a sharded blob store on SQLite that speaks the Redis protocol. Zerodha's engineering post introduces Blobasaur, written in Rust, which replaced an unmaintained single-node SSDB setup for storing user layout and preference blobs. These JSON blobs range from kilobytes to megabytes. The company says it handles thousands of reads and writes per second with single-digit millisecond latency on commodity hardware, after it rejected ScyllaDB, PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS and S3 for this workload (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters ask about replication, fault tolerance and the consistency model when a node fails, saying they could not find these covered in the post or repository.
  • One suggests mapping JSON schemas into SQL tables so that incremental updates avoid rewriting whole blobs.

Compressing memory with zram can postpone RAM upgrades on Linux. A blog post shows zram on a 32GB workstation fitting 5.7GB of data into 1.7GB of RAM, a ratio of about 3.35 to 1, at some CPU and latency cost. The post notes that Fedora and Pop!_OS enable this by default but Ubuntu does not. After the HN thread, the author added an update recommending zswap for most setups (HN discussion).

  • Commenters explain the difference: zswap sits in front of disk swap and moves cold pages to disk automatically, while zram is a compressed block device with a hard capacity limit.

PHP 8.6 is released. The release page lists partial function application using placeholder arguments and a nanosecond-precision \Time\Duration class. It also adds an Io\Poll API built on epoll, kqueue and similar mechanisms, intended to get past stream_select()'s limits for event-loop libraries. Other additions are a clamp() function, a SortDirection enum, and default values for readonly properties (HN discussion).

  • One commenter highlights reduced overhead for PHP's thread-safe (ZTS) build, which could eventually make native async support more practical.
  • Others note that the PHP team announced a separate critical security fix for existing versions around the same time, and advise patching first.

An industry outlook expects SSD prices to ease in the second half of 2027, with hard drives later. A September post on a storage-app vendor's blog cites ComputerBase tracking that shows hard drives about 134% and SSDs about 129% above September 2025 prices, though monthly increases are shrinking. It points to TrendForce's forecast that the NAND shortage will end in the second half of 2027. Hard drive capacity, by contrast, is largely contracted to data centers into 2028 (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters are skeptical of the article's framing, and others doubt that lower manufacturing costs will lead to lower retail prices.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 18, 2026
item.description:
Two widely deployed server components received critical security fixes, while new research looks at how AI is changing search traffic, code review, and auditing.

Two critical remote code execution flaws were disclosed in NGINX's HTTP/2 handling. According to Wiz's write-up, CVE-2026-123633 (a use-after-free) and CVE-2026-123007 (an integer underflow present since NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015) both carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. Both require HTTP/2 to be enabled, and they were found independently by five research groups, with Wiz saying it used AI tooling for discovery and validation. F5 shipped fixes in a coordinated release on November 18 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters first questioned why so much detail was published before patched builds were visible, then noted the new versions appeared within about 30 minutes.
  • Several observed that past NGINX vulnerabilities have also clustered around HTTP/2, and that HTTP/1.1-only deployments are outside the stated preconditions for these two flaws.

A memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder can lead to remote code execution. Calif's disclosure of CVE-2026-114938 places the bug in hand-written AVX-512 VBMI assembly used on x86-64. A malformed input as short as 64 "A" characters followed by "=" causes a write past the end of the output array. The researchers report pre-authentication RCE against default configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and say AI assistance let them find the bug and build a first exploit in about three hours, for under $200 in tokens (HN discussion).

  • Commenters relayed unconfirmed reports that running Java with -XX:UseAVX=2 avoids the vulnerable code path as a temporary workaround.
  • A link to the corresponding OpenJDK fix commit was shared for those checking whether their builds are patched.

A randomized experiment finds Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to outside websites by about 40%. A Revscope analysis summarizes a working paper in which US desktop Chrome users were randomly assigned to have Overviews hidden or shown. On searches that would show an Overview, users who saw it made 0.37 outbound clicks per search, compared with 0.62 for users who didn't, while ad clicks were unchanged. Separate DataForSEO data shows Overviews on 61% of tracked US keywords in August 2026, up from about 6% two years earlier. The paper has not been peer reviewed and covers desktop only (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters note that organic results were already being pushed down by ads and SEO-driven content well before AI answers appeared.
  • Others argue that if Google withheld AI answers, users would likely go to other LLM products instead, some of which are now adding ads of their own.

A Harvard working paper finds AI coding agents increased code output but not finished work. As reported by ComplexDiscovery, Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton used engineering-analytics data from 718 firms. Agent adoption raised lines of code by about 30%, but resolved issues did not rise measurably, and getting code through review took 49% longer. The paper is a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters argue the binding constraint is still unclear upfront specification rather than review itself.
  • Others suggest the finding raises the value of engineers who can read and critically analyze code they did not write.

KPMG UK says AI agents sometimes probed issues more deeply than its human team in a trial audit. According to European Business Magazine, citing the Financial Times, the effort was codenamed Project Exponential. More than 100 agents worked alongside a conventional audit team on an unnamed FTSE 250 company's accounts, gathering data, drafting conclusions, and suggesting next steps. KPMG's UK head of audit said the agents in several instances raised questions the human auditors had not (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters suggest the result may say as much about the incentives and depth of Big Four audits, pointing to past accounting scandals such as Enron, as about AI capability.
  • Others note that AI tends to perform well in domains with fixed, well-defined procedures, which may describe much of auditing.

Researchers propose Energy-Based Reasoners, small looped models that solve constraint puzzles with far less inference compute. The project page from Duke, UIUC, and Harvard researchers describes models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and refine their answers by gradient descent on it. The gradient also serves as a stopping signal. With 1.8M parameters, the model reaches 99.9% on Sudoku-Extreme using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model (the headline's 385× figure does not match the page), and it reports state-of-the-art solution coverage on N-Queens and graph coloring (HN discussion).

  • Commenters stress that the benchmarks are tightly constrained puzzles with few valid solutions, and that "reasoning" here differs from what LLM reasoning models do.
  • Some suggest testing on open-ended games like chess or Go would better show whether the efficiency gains generalize.

Microsoft announced seven new MAI models positioned on price-performance. The Ignite announcement covers models for coding, security, image editing, realtime speech, transcription, and decision-making. Each is compared against OpenAI and Anthropic models on cost and quality, using Microsoft's own figures. Microsoft also said its second-generation Maia 200 accelerator is now in production running its largest models (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point out that the weights are closed, technical detail is limited, and the models are not yet listed in independent indexes such as Artificial Analysis.
  • Some question the usefulness of comparisons like pitting a specialized decision model against a general frontier model.

SolidJS 2.0 reached stable after five years of development. The release post describes async support built into the reactive graph, so computations can return promises or async iterators. Server functions, including streaming "live" functions over Server-Sent Events, now live in Solid's core. Development builds report reactivity mistakes with stable error codes, source locations, and repair guides aimed at coding agents (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that the ecosystem of ready-made component libraries for Solid is still relatively thin.
  • One observes that the "built for agents" diagnostics are simply better debugging output that helps human developers equally.

Phrack published issue 73. The new issue, released November 17, includes technical articles on escaping Docker containers via vDSO, escaping the Chromium renderer sandbox through Skia, kernel exploit development with LLMs, and backdoor attacks against machine learning. It also adds history pieces on the 2000 SSH1 exploit and a 2003 Linux kernel backdoor (HN discussion).

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 17, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers a large third-party script compromise, an outage traced to patching, new findings on Windows telemetry, and coding-model and agent-tooling releases, plus longer reads on display gamma, chemistry, and free course material.

Malicious code was served to 178 organisations' websites through Optimizely. According to a Report URI analysis, on 16 November an attacker inserted code into the "Project JavaScript" field of Optimizely Web customer snippets. Affected sites included Zoom, the BBC, GitLab and HSBC. The payload swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies, and delivered iOS exploit kits to older iPhones. Most infected snippets were cleaned by that evening, and the report says it is not yet known how the attacker got write access across unrelated customer projects (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to earlier incidents of the same kind and argue that compromises of third-party tag scripts are a known, recurring risk rather than a new one.
  • Others note that Optimizely's own status page showed only a partial outage affecting recommendations tracking and reporting while this was happening.

The NSA's internal classified network went down after a software patch. CNN reports that NSANet, the agency's internal network for classified communications, was down and the campus was limited to essential personnel. The agency described the problem as degradation during scheduled maintenance. The Director of National Intelligence attributed it to systems not coming back up after patches for PHP vulnerabilities disclosed last month, and sources said there was no evidence of a cyberattack (HN discussion).

A Windows 11 diagnostics component records which coding agents and developer tools are used. A reverse-engineering write-up found that MissionControlAggregator.dll checks for executables such as codex.exe, claude.exe, cursor.exe, python.exe and gcc.exe. It records which ones were observed as a bitmap and sends that in a diagnostic report, which is uploaded unless the user opts out of optional diagnostic data. The author found the feature already enabled on a test VM and found no prompt text or source code in the report (HN discussion).

Microsoft released two lower-cost coding models, MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash. Microsoft's announcement positions them for everyday enterprise coding. It claims that, averaged over four benchmarks, MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost. Microsoft says the models are not yet tuned for harder work such as long-horizon agentic tasks (HN discussion).

  • Commenters ask whether the models were trained from scratch or built by applying reinforcement learning to existing open models, which the discussion does not resolve.

A benchmark finds that the most cost-effective agent harness depends on the model. Runta's FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 ran 22 harness configurations against 5 open-weight models on 62 terminal tasks, for 27,280 runs in total. Each model had a different best-value harness. For example, Codex CLI ranked first on cost with GLM-5.3 but 16th with Kimi-K3 (HN discussion).

  • The founder notes in the thread that the evaluation runs on their company's own runtime, and commenters clarify that "failed" runs means tasks that missed pass criteria, not runtime crashes.
  • One commenter argues that explaining cost through steps per pass is close to circular, and another asks why harness-specific fine-tuning of open models was not considered.

OpenCode released Browse, a tool that lets coding agents use a person's existing browser. Browse combines an MCP server with a Chromium extension. Agents work in background tabs with the user's existing logins, and they hand a tab back to the user for steps like 2FA or payments. It supports several Chromium-based browsers and any MCP client (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that Playwright's MCP server and Chrome's DevTools MCP already overlap with this, and some advise using separate browser profiles to limit the security risk of giving agents logged-in sessions.
  • One user reports frequent disconnections that require re-pairing, and others note that Firefox is not supported.

John Carmack explained why early 3dfx cards produced washed-out colours. In a post, Carmack writes that 3dfx and NeXT deliberately used near-linear colour output. With only 4–6 bits per channel, that produced visible banding in dark tones. Textures authored on conventional non-linear displays also looked washed out on these cards (HN discussion).

  • A commenter gives figures: CRTs have a gamma of roughly 2.2, standard VGA applied no correction, and 3dfx defaulted to about 1.5, so 3dfx was closer to linear but still not fully corrected.
  • Another notes that sRGB values do map linearly to CRT signal voltage, even though they do not map linearly to light intensity.

An essay introduces chemical reaction network theory, which studies reactions through network structure. The article walks through Martin Feinberg's deficiency theorems for a beginner audience. It explains how the structure of a reaction network can predict qualitative behaviour, such as oscillation, without estimating hundreds of rate constants. It uses examples like the Belousov–Zhabotinsky and Briggs–Rauscher oscillators (HN discussion).

  • Some commenters caution that the geometric framing is a useful modelling abstraction rather than a full account of chemistry, which they say ultimately reduces to quantum electrodynamics.

Carnegie Mellon is publishing full semesters of computer science lectures on YouTube. The new CS Learn site lists courses including Machine Learning Systems, AI Agents and Machine Learning in Production. More courses are scheduled for January 2027, and self-paced courseware is planned next (HN discussion).

  • The program's lead says in the thread that MIT did something similar 25 years ago, and that the new part is student-built tooling that automates much of the video production.
  • A commenter recalls that many universities removed free lecture videos in the early 2010s over accessibility liability, before automatic captioning was available.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 16, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers infrastructure reliability and trust: a cloud outage postmortem, two web security issues, and how far a formal proof can be trusted, along with new developer tools and a farming study.

Microsoft traces its multi-day email outage to a defect introduced in a July update. According to a preliminary incident report covered by The Register, a change to Microsoft 365 network gateway servers caused lock contention in an internal Windows process. The problem got worse on newer machines with more cores, while load testing had focused on weaker hardware. A Teams failover arrived while about 14 percent of gateway capacity was out of service, and the combined load pushed more than 80 percent of servers into an unresponsive state. Because the defect was months old, engineers could not simply roll it back and instead shipped an update restoring the earlier code path (HN discussion).

  • Commenters question whether testing on hardware weaker than production is an acceptable trade-off, since the concurrency bug only appeared on higher-spec machines.

An email-only pool alarm went unseen during the outage, and 15 hotel guests were hurt by excess chlorine. WDR reports that an automatic dosing system at Phantasialand's Hotel Ling Bao in Brühl pumped too much chlorine into a pool. The maintenance system's email alerts never arrived, so no one acted on them; four guests went to hospital and one stayed for observation. A cybersecurity architect quoted in the piece places responsibility on the installation, which had no second alerting channel (HN discussion).

  • Commenters broadly describe the outage as a proximate rather than root cause, and argue that alarms for hazardous systems should be minimal, local and redundant rather than depend on a large cloud service.

A researcher disclosed a now-fixed universal XSS flaw in uBlock Origin's element picker. In a detailed writeup, the researcher shows how a malicious page could leak the Firefox extension's per-install UUID through a default filter rule. The page could then embed the picker in an invisible iframe and drive it with messages. A newline injected into the filter options added a trusted scriptlet filter, and a single user click could then run arbitrary JavaScript on any site. The MV3 uBO Lite version had a related but less serious issue. The fix includes a secret that the real picker must present, and the author says an AI model found the core issue, which they then verified (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters note that the UUID leak alone could serve as a tracking identifier, and point to an earlier report of Firefox extensions leaking their install IDs the same way.
  • Others note a structural weakness: extensions that place their interfaces inside a page's DOM, such as password managers, can expose information to the page they run on.

Old Bitly short links in years-old corporate posts were re-registered and redirected. Ransomnews found that links in 2011 posts from Burger King and McDonald's had been newly created by other parties and pointed to unrelated pages, even though Bitly's help pages say link endings cannot be reused. Neither company's account was compromised. Bitly confirmed the issue, suspended the accounts involved and began disabling affected links (HN discussion).

  • One commenter describes a related tactic: spammers buy lapsed domains that reputable organizations still point to via CNAME records, which makes spam links look trustworthy.
  • Others note that short links hide their destination, which adds risk when people run patterns like piping a fetched script straight into a shell.

A Lean community blog explains what "checked in Lean" does and doesn't guarantee. The Xena Project post sets out questions to ask of AI-generated Lean code. The first is whether the formal statement actually matches the paper's claim, which can mean reading thousands of lines of supporting definitions. The second is whether the code compiles in a trusted setting. It notes that about 38 of the 290 papers with Lean code in OpenAI's recent theorem release do not formally state their main theorem, and it warns against running untrusted Lean code without a sandbox (HN discussion).

  • Commenters compare it to code that compiles but doesn't do what was intended: a valid proof may not prove the intended claim.
  • Some ask why Lean can execute arbitrary code at all, and others observe that LLM-written Lean tends to be much longer than needed even for simple statements.

Jiff, a Rust datetime library, reaches version 1.0. Author Andrew Gallant's announcement describes an API built around time zones so that daylight saving time is handled correctly by default. It notes that Jiff is already used in projects such as uv, Cargo, Starship and Jujutsu. Gallant commits to keeping 1.0 stable indefinitely unless a significant defect is found, so other libraries can safely expose it in their public APIs (HN discussion).

Self-hosting world map tiles with PMTiles now costs a few dollars a month. A walkthrough explains how Protomaps' PMTiles format stores a whole tileset in a single file that clients read via HTTP Range requests, so it can be served from a storage bucket and CDN. The author estimates that the 139GB world map costs about $5 a month to store on Bunny.net with replication. They also estimate per-load costs well below commercial map APIs, though actual bandwidth varies by user (HN discussion).

  • One commenter cautions that this only applies to vector basemaps: high-resolution satellite imagery quickly reaches hundreds of terabytes, which forced them to stop at zoom level 17.
  • Another describes moving a mapping app from a paid tile provider to Protomaps after bills reached about €150 a month, and notes that self-hosting also lets them customize what goes into the tiles.

Cornell studies find that low sheep stocking rates on solar farms increase beneficial insects. In research described by Cornell, grazing two sheep per hectare around solar arrays raised the number of bees and lady beetles by 38 percent compared with mowing, mostly due to more honey bees. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation control was most effective but honey bee numbers fell by 45 percent. A separate paper introduces a spreadsheet tool to help farmers plan flock size and contracts for solar grazing (HN discussion).

  • Commenters place this within the broader field of agrivoltaics, citing earlier work on panels that let some light wavelengths through to crops growing underneath.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 15, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers a spaceflight milestone, a memory-chip antitrust ruling, a display-comfort issue on Apple's newest laptops, a license-plate surveillance case, and several substantive reads for programmers and the scientifically curious.

SpaceX caught the Starship vehicle at the end of Flight 15. According to the company's launch page, Starship Flight 15 ended with the ship being caught on return, and the submission linked to SpaceX's post and the launch video. The source material gives no further technical detail about the flight (HN discussion).

A federal judge declined to dismiss a DRAM supply-conspiracy suit against Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. On Nov. 14, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise of the Northern District of California denied the companies' joint motion to dismiss a proposed class action alleging they coordinated cuts to conventional DRAM such as DDR5 while shifting capacity to HBM for AI accelerators, LitNews reports. The judge distinguished the Ninth Circuit's 2022 DRAM II decision and pointed to long-term HBM lock-ups, refused conventional DRAM contracts, Micron's closure of its Crucial brand, and the absence of expansion despite record prices. She gave no weight to investor talk of "supply discipline," industry-conference meetings, or the three-firm market structure. The allegations are unproven, and answers are due Dec. 7 (HN discussion).

  • One commenter questions the theory, arguing that moving from DDR4 to DDR5 is a genuine product transition and that Chinese manufacturers can still supply DDR4.
  • A researcher describes the practical effect: a planned workstation with 256 GB of RAM now costs several thousand dollars for memory alone.

Apple's new OLED MacBook Pro uses low-frequency PWM dimming, and some users report discomfort. A MacAnorak article collects forum and Reddit reports of headaches, eye fatigue, and dizziness with the new "PROLED XDR" display. It cites Notebookcheck measurements of 240Hz PWM at brightness settings of 99% and below, compared with 14,880Hz on the Mini-LED M4 Pro model, which Apple still sells. The author cautions that frequency is only one factor and that not every complaint is necessarily caused by PWM (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point to a peer-reviewed study in Scientific Reports finding that people can perceive flicker at frequencies well above a display's refresh rate.
  • Several note that nobody knows how common PWM sensitivity is, and they call for research to quantify it.

EFF and the ACLU asked a federal appeals court to require warrants for license-plate-reader searches. The EFF's amicus brief in the Sixth Circuit case United States v. Sturdivant concerns Cleveland-area robberies in which police ran open-ended searches of the Flock and ELSAG databases to identify a suspect's car. The district court had ruled that a visible license plate carries no reasonable expectation of privacy. The brief argues that networked ALPR tracking is a Fourth Amendment "search" (HN discussion).

  • Commenters cite New Hampshire's existing law as a model: it bans collecting plates for later analysis and requires non-matching images to be deleted within three minutes without leaving the device.
  • Others go further and argue that ALPR systems should only retain hits on plates tied to an active warrant.

Sebastian Raschka published a detailed walkthrough of positional embeddings in LLMs. The article explains why transformers need explicit position information. It compares GPT-2's learned absolute embeddings, which are added before the first block, with RoPE, which is applied inside attention in models like MiniMax-M3. It includes a small PyTorch implementation and a survey of the approaches used by 2026 open-weight models (HN discussion).

  • A commenter offers a theoretical lens the article does not: positional embeddings can be understood as group representations, with RoPE representing the translation group, and this framing explains how such embeddings are derived and made learnable.

The C++ language server clice reached version 1.0. According to the release post, clice is a Clang-based C/C++ language server written in C++23. It compiles code in an isolated process pool, so a compiler crash does not bring down the whole server, as it can with clangd. It also supports C++20 named modules, with on-disk caching of PCH and PCM files across sessions. The release follows about four months of nightly alpha builds and roughly 1,000 commits (HN discussion).

  • One commenter notes that Clang-based indexers remain far slower on very large codebases than older non-Clang indexers in Eclipse and Qt Creator, and says they would accept less precision in exchange for speed.
  • Another observes that the release's comparison demo shows clice crashing at the same point as clangd, but in an isolated worker process rather than taking down the server.

Crows responded to visual decision tasks about twice as fast as humans and monkeys in a new study. Research published in Science and reported by The New York Times tested two carrion crows on judging whether dots on a screen moved left or right. The researchers describe the result as the first measurement of the neural speed of avian decision-making (HN discussion).

  • A commenter points out that the "birdbrain" insult refers to intelligence, not speed, so a faster reaction time does not directly rebut it.

LinkedIn and Monster removed about 1,500 misleading job ads after a CBC investigation linked them to a multi-level marketing company. CBC found that remote "travel planner" listings advertising salaries up to $75,000 US led applicants to Evolution Travel. Applicants were asked to pay hundreds of dollars upfront plus a monthly fee, and there was no actual job. LinkedIn removed close to 900 ads and barred the companies behind them from posting, while Monster removed 600 (HN discussion).

  • Commenters place this within a broader pattern of scam advertising on major platforms, and some argue that one-off takedowns need to become sustained policy enforcement against ghost listings.

A developer documented building a NES emulator in the Odin language. lucyNES is a solo project, built over about seven months, that runs Battletoads and hundreds of other games. It supports seven cartridge mappers, save states, a debugger, and partial sound. The author writes that reaching a basic working state was fast, but the final 10% of accuracy took most of the effort, especially CPU–PPU timing and mapper behavior. Odin's lack of automatic integer promotion caused several bugs (HN discussion).

  • One commenter notes a practical limitation: Odin depends on recent LLVM versions, which makes programs written in it harder to build on older or legacy systems.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 14, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers a shorter disclosure deadline for software bugs, a data-exposure study of AI-built web apps, an air traffic control outage, and several releases from the machine learning and developer tooling world.

Google Project Zero is shortening its vulnerability disclosure deadline in stages. Since 2021, Project Zero has given vendors 90 days to fix a bug, plus 30 days for patch rollout. Under its new "Full X" policy, details are now published 90 days after reporting. That drops to 60 days on February 2, 2027 and to 30 days on January 3, 2028, and most grace-period exceptions are removed. The team says AI-assisted tools have sped up both bug discovery and exploitation from patches, and that it now finds several vulnerabilities a week in targets that once yielded a few a year (HN discussion).

  • Commenters expect downstream Linux distributions such as Ubuntu to have trouble shipping fixes within the shorter windows.
  • Some suggest that organizations using AI to find bugs should give vendors and open-source maintainers the same tools to help them fix those bugs.

A study finds sensitive data exposed in many apps built with Lovable. Researchers examined 159,041 Lovable projects found through Common Crawl. Of the 24,664 that loaded Supabase data without a login, 7,403 (about 30%) had tables containing email addresses that further read-only requests could reach. The authors caution that this figure is not a confirmed leak rate. The specific cases they found include more than 80,000 forum profiles with over 200,000 chat messages, and more than 1,000 records with passport details (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that misconfigured databases are not new. They argue that AI-built apps are easier targets because they appear in large numbers and can often be probed by inspecting browser network requests.

An equipment failure caused a nationwide FAA ground stop lasting more than four hours. The FAA halted all U.S. departures at 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday after controllers saw inconsistencies in radar data and aircraft communications. It lifted the stop at 8:15 p.m. ET, NBC News reports. The FAA said a router sent too much data and overloaded older air traffic control equipment, and officials said they had found no evidence of a cyberattack. More than 7,000 flights were canceled Friday, and FlightAware logged over 3,700 more cancellations by Saturday morning (HN discussion).

  • Commenters shared the original FAA advisory, which gave only "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety" as the cause. One passenger reported that their captain did not know what the order meant at first.

ggml, the tensor library behind llama.cpp, reaches version 1.0. The 1.0.0 release removes the deprecated public API and some legacy operations, adds FP8 support and configurable YaRN truncation, and bumps the RPC protocol so that incompatible peers are rejected. It also includes performance work across CUDA, Metal, Vulkan, SYCL, OpenCL, WebGPU and Hexagon backends, much of it aimed at mixture-of-experts models and FlashAttention (HN discussion).

  • One user reports steady speed gains of roughly 5–10% from monthly upgrades on the same hardware. Their 50K-token benchmark dropped from 4:22 to 3:59 after this update.
  • Another says ggml's Vulkan backend is what makes local inference usable on their older AMD card.

PyPI project pages now show whether release files can be traced to their source. PyPI has finished its redesign of project pages, adding a security tab that shows each file's attestations. The tab labels a release as having full or no provenance, and it warns when provenance is incomplete, inconsistent, changed, or lost compared with earlier releases. The design follows the OpenSSF Attestations Style Guide (HN discussion).

  • Commenters stress that these signals help detect hijacked releases of legitimate projects, but do not identify packages that were malicious from the start.
  • Some maintainers point out that publishing only some files through Trusted Publishing triggers a warning. Others ask how self-hosted builds or smaller forges such as Codeberg could produce attestations.

A proposed terminal protocol would draw borders on cell edges instead of using character cells. Ratatui's maintainer describes a cell attribute that lets a terminal draw thin lines along the edges of character cells. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments with their own color and style, so panels no longer give up a row and column on each side. The author has a working patch for Ghostty, has built demo apps, and is asking terminal and TUI authors for feedback (HN discussion).

  • One commenter points to an existing approach: overstrike mode (DECSET 20), which lets border characters be drawn over text cells but is supported by few terminals other than mintty.
  • Others question why the author says the feature would not work through multiplexers like tmux, since other cell attributes pass through without problems.

A developer reimplements DeepSeek V3's architecture in about 190 lines of JAX. The Show HN project implements four core ideas from the DeepSeek V3 paper in plain JAX with no framework: multi-head latent attention, a mixture-of-experts design, load balancing without an auxiliary loss, and multi-token prediction. A 36.2M-parameter version trained in about 2.6 hours on a MacBook Air. Turning on the bias-based balancing evened out expert usage without changing validation loss (HN discussion).

  • One commenter reports running it end to end on an AMD RX 7600 XT under ROCm. They note that JAX's plugin rejected the card's architecture until they set an environment variable override.

Removing the enzyme granzyme K reduced signs of organ ageing in mice. According to a Nature research highlight, aged mice engineered to lack granzyme K had better heart and liver function and less kidney damage. The underlying study appears in Immunity. Its authors suggest that drugs lowering the enzyme might one day reduce ageing effects without weakening immune defences (HN discussion).

  • Commenters quoting the paper's abstract note that immune ageing still occurred in these mice. The authors describe the enzyme as a driver of tissue ageing, not of immune ageing or systemic inflammation.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 13, 2026
item.description:
Friday was shaped by a long Microsoft 365 outage and a shorter Claude disruption, alongside two data-exposure disclosures, a new payment model for search APIs, and some systems-programming reading old and new.

Microsoft 365 suffered a prolonged global email and collaboration outage. According to Microsoft's status updates, Exchange Online connectivity problems began in the Americas on November 12 and later affected users in any region. Microsoft said the cause was not a traffic increase but servers failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the remaining capacity. CNN reports that Outlook, Teams and Copilot were disrupted, that Microsoft attributed the outage to a technical issue rather than a security breach, and that email queues were later "approaching normal levels" (HN discussion, second HN discussion).

  • Users with email-based two-factor authentication describe being locked out of unrelated accounts, a reminder that an email outage can spread to other services.
  • One commenter calculates that this incident alone pulls Office 365's uptime for the year down to roughly three nines, and notes that customers may be able to claim SLA credits.

Claude services had a roughly two-hour authentication incident. Anthropic's status page shows an investigation into users failing to authenticate to claude.ai and Claude Code starting at 09:58 UTC on November 13. A fix was deployed around 11:05 and the incident was marked resolved at 11:58. Affected services included claude.ai, the Claude Console, Claude Code and Claude Cowork (HN discussion, second HN discussion).

  • Users reported existing sessions suddenly requiring re-login and then failing with OAuth errors. Some commenters suspect a link to the concurrent Microsoft outage, but the status page does not state a cause.

TSMC reported that employee data appeared online and said it found no compromise of its own systems. In a statement filed with the SEC, the chipmaker said data on current and former employees was posted on an external website without authorization. TSMC said the data matches records held with a cloud service provider and is unrelated to operations or customer data (HN discussion).

  • Commenters point out that the "TSMC Hacked" headline overstates the filing, since the company describes exposed employee data, possibly via a third party, rather than a breach of its systems.
  • A commenter cites outside reporting that the leakers claim about 6.9GB covering roughly 46,000 employee records and are seeking a ransom. TSMC's statement does not confirm this.

A Brazilian insurer disclosed a breach affecting names and tax IDs of all 7.6 million customers. The incident involves Caixa's insurance arm and was disclosed in a company filing. According to the headline, the exposed data consists of names and Brazilian tax ID (CPF) numbers (HN discussion).

  • Commenters from Brazil explain that the CPF is not treated as a secret like a US Social Security number. It is routinely requested by pharmacies, gyms and shops, and earlier leaks mean it is already widely available.
  • Others note that many of Caixa's customers are not tech-savvy, so the main risk is follow-on phishing and fraud. The company is also unrelated to the Catalan bank "la Caixa."

Brave's Search API now accepts per-request stablecoin payments from AI agents. Brave announced support for the x402 protocol. A request sent without payment gets an HTTP 402 response stating the price, and the agent then retries with a signed USDC payment on the Base blockchain, so no account or API key is required. Pricing matches Brave's published rate of $0.005 per request, and gas fees are covered for a limited time (HN discussion).

  • A commenter who runs agents notes that agents often rephrase and repeat searches, and each retry is a separate paid call. Without an API key there is no monthly bill to reveal this, so per-agent budget limits matter.
  • Several see per-query micropayments as a possible alternative to ad-funded search, noting that card networks were asked for this kind of model decades ago.

Eli Lilly's CEO said AI is unlikely to cure major diseases within a decade. A post by Gary Marcus collects responses to an IPO-related video in which Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicted that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease and mental illness would be cured within ten years. Lilly CEO Dave Ricks responded that biology remains largely unmapped, that randomized human trials are the main bottleneck, and that progress will likely be "steady and incremental." Researchers including Eric Topol made similar points (HN discussion).

  • Commenters stress that drug development is limited mainly by lab work, manufacturing and clinical testing rather than by software. For slow-moving cancers, even finding out whether a therapy is working can take years.

A C programmer explains why they now write new systems code in Zig. In this post, Mihalis Tsoukalos compares C's goto-based cleanup with Zig's errdefer, which sits next to each allocation. He shows how a testing allocator can exercise every failure path, and how slices that carry their length turn a silent off-by-one read in C into a bounds-check panic. He also covers compiler-enforced error handling and replacing the preprocessor with comptime (HN discussion).

  • Commenters note that C code can partly enforce error checking with warn_unused_result in GCC and Clang, or [[nodiscard]], and that D and Nim have offered many of these features for years.

Andy Hertzfeld's account of building Switcher, the Mac's first multitasking environment, resurfaced. The Folklore.org story describes how, in October 1984, Hertzfeld watched a journalist switch instantly between programs on a PC using a DOS utility and realized the new 512K Macintosh could do the same. Making it work meant giving each application its own heap zone and working out exactly which low-memory system globals had to be swapped on every switch (HN discussion).

  • One commenter, a developer from that era, could not find any record of a DOS utility called "Memory Shift" and wonders whether the story describes something like Borland's Sidekick, also released in 1984.

IceWM, a lightweight X11 window manager first released in 1997, is still actively maintained. The project site describes a fast, keyboard-friendly window manager with a built-in taskbar, multiple workspaces, more than 450 downloadable themes and translations into about three dozen languages. The latest release is 4.1.0, from August 2026 (HN discussion).

  • One user still runs it today as a low-resource desktop for a headless remote-desktop machine, valuing that the panel, menu and window manager work together without configuration.
  • A former distribution developer recalls shipping IceWM as a commercial Linux desktop's default in 2004–2005, with GNOME's Nautilus drawing the desktop icons.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 12, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers a leadership change at Nvidia, a widely deployed web server patch, a CPU architecture interview, and several smaller software projects.

Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia's CEO, and CFO Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Nvidia's board announced that Huang left his roles as President, CEO and board member effective immediately. Kress will keep her CFO role while the board runs a search that will consider internal and external candidates. Former Synopsys CEO Harvey C. Jones was named the company's first-ever board chair, and third-quarter results remain scheduled for November 17 (HN discussion). BBC coverage reports that the resignation followed reports about Huang's personal relationships, and that the shares fell more than 13% at the open before recovering some ground (HN discussion).

Anthropic has opened an initial public offering page. The IPO site says little beyond the fact of the offering. It notes that the UK retail offer is facilitated by RetailBook, which is regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (HN discussion).

  • One commenter reports that a retail brokerage's IPO page is available only in the UK and a limited set of European countries, so not all investors can take part.
  • Others place the listing alongside other very large recent or expected tech IPOs and ask how institutional investors will make room for them.

Apache HTTP Server versions 2.4.55 through 2.4.70 have a critical race condition in the HTTP/2 module. According to Wiz's write-up, a synchronization flaw in mod_http2's assign_headers() function can let a remote, unauthenticated attacker corrupt heap memory and potentially execute code. The fix is in 2.4.71, and disabling HTTP/2 is the suggested stopgap. At publication there was no public exploit and no reported exploitation (HN discussion).

  • Commenters question whether heap corruption automatically means remote code execution, since many memory-safety bugs are hard to turn into a working exploit.
  • Several flag inconsistencies in the advisory, including a second CVE number in the text and GitHub being listed as the "vendor" of the mod_h2 module.

Users report security regressions after a Humble Bundle site rewrite. A forum thread says the storefront's redesign weakened account security. The thread attributes the rewrite to AI-generated code, though the provided material does not detail how it was built (HN discussion).

  • One commenter says they could log in without being asked for their second factor, and another says emailed login codes arrived about an hour late.
  • Several argue the problem lies with staffing and review decisions rather than the AI tools themselves.

A 2016 essay explains why writing correct software is fundamentally hard. Ron Pressler's extended talk collects results from computability and complexity theory. It starts with the halting theorem and Rice's theorem and argues that verification has unavoidable costs, whatever the tooling (HN discussion).

  • Commenters stress that software has to be designed to be verifiable in the first place, which they see as the hard part, including when AI is used to write proofs.
  • Others separate mathematical correctness from behaving well in messy real-world conditions, and say the practical skill is knowing when formal methods are worth the cost.

An abandoned Quake 4 expansion has been completed by modders and released. The project is distributed as OpenQ4 0.14.1 for Windows x64 on ModDB (HN discussion).

  • The discussion suggests AI tools helped finish the project, which led some to compare it with posthumous releases of unfinished creative work.

AMD's Mike Clark explains the design choices in Zen 6 and Zen 6c. In a Chips and Cheese interview, Clark says the dense Zen 6c core is now the top performance core, with 4MB of L3 per core and larger internal queues made possible by its lower frequency target. He also covers dropping from three integer multipliers to two, adding VNNI units late in the design, and enabling four 256-bit vector loads (HN discussion).

A developer is building an open-source pinball simulation engine for Linux. The project update describes a new sound system, revised physics now running on the Jolt engine, an in-game table editor, multiple camera modes, and TypeScript scripting for table logic. The author plans to show it to vendors at an industry expo (HN discussion).

  • In the thread, the author says the engine builds on their long-standing Pascal Tiny.Sim library. Tables are designed in parametric CAD, imported as 3D meshes, and simplified into primitive physics bodies.

item.title: HN Mindful Digest — November 11, 2026
item.description:
Today's briefing covers privacy and security engineering, hardware research, and a few AI claims that look more modest on closer analysis.

An analysis argues that a widely reported AI weight-editing result is mostly a linear program. MIT CSAIL's "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming" reported that GPT-6 Astra raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% by editing 0.016% of its weights. The edit mainly stops the small model from getting stuck in repetitive "thinking loops." In a new write-up, Nathan Barry shows that the edit is a rank-1 change and that choosing it can be framed as a linear program. Astra searched for about 8 hours, while a couple of LP solves of roughly a minute each produce a comparable edit that changes 8× fewer weights (HN discussion).

  • Several commenters say the analysis tempers earlier headlines: Astra looks less like a model that reads weights directly and more like one running ordinary model-editing experiments.
  • Others note the technique resembles existing "refusal direction" ablation methods used to uncensor models, which the model may have seen in its training data.

A researcher used voltage glitching to unlock disabled hardware on an NVIDIA mining card.
